blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Unit 9 (Inverse Trigonometric (TOC: 'Inverse Trigonometric Functions and Their Graphs')), arranged by the unit's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each one is solved briefly, step by step.
9.1 Inverse Trigonometric Functions and their Graph

blocks.prompt: 1 When does a function \(f : X \to Y\) have an inverse? How are the domain and range of \(f^{-1}\) related to those of \(f\)?
blocks.explanation: Only when \(f\) is one-to-one and onto (bijective). Then \(f^{-1} : Y \to X\), with domain of \(f^{-1}\) = range of \(f\) and range of \(f^{-1}\) = domain of \(f\); \(f^{-1}(y) = x\) when \(f(x) = y\).

book_ref.quote: only a one-to-one and onto function will have an inverse

blocks.prompt: 2 Why do the trigonometric functions have no inverses on their whole domains? How is this put right?
blocks.explanation: They are periodic, so many angles give the same value (e.g. \(\sin\frac{\pi}{4} = \sin\frac{3\pi}{4}\)); they are not one-to-one. We restrict the domain to one interval where each value is taken once, and take the codomain equal to the set of values (e.g. \([-1, 1]\)); the function becomes bijective and has an inverse.

book_ref.quote: by carefully restricting their domains and codomains, we can make these functions bijective

blocks.prompt: 3 Write \(\cos\frac{2\pi}{3} = -\frac{1}{2}\) in inverse form and state how it is read.
blocks.explanation: \(\frac{2\pi}{3} = \cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\) (since \(y = \cos^{-1} x\) iff \(x = \cos y\), and \(\frac{2\pi}{3} \in [0, \pi]\)). Read: '\(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) is equal to cosine inverse of \(-\frac{1}{2}\)' (arccosine of \(-\frac{1}{2}\)).

book_ref.quote: Similarly, we can write the other equations as

blocks.prompt: 4 What is meant by the principal value of \(\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{2}\)? Why is \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) not its value?
blocks.explanation: Many angles have sine \(\frac{1}{2}\) (\(\frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{5\pi}{6}, \frac{13\pi}{6}, \dots\)). The principal value is the one angle in the standard interval \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\): \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) is outside that interval.

book_ref.quote: The single angle chosen in this way is called the principal value.

blocks.prompt: 5 Define the principal sine function and the inverse sine function. Give the domain and range of the inverse sine function.
blocks.explanation: Principal sine function: \(\sin : \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \to [-1, 1]\), which is bijective. Inverse sine: \(y = \sin^{-1} x\) iff \(x = \sin y\); domain \([-1, 1]\), range \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).

book_ref.quote: is called the principal sine function

blocks.prompt: 6 Find the principal values of \(\sin^{-1}(-1)\) and \(\sin^{-1} 0\).
blocks.explanation: \(\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -1\) with \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\) in the range, so \(\sin^{-1}(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{2}\). \(\sin 0 = 0\), so \(\sin^{-1} 0 = 0\).

book_ref.quote: This is the test for every answer

blocks.prompt: 7 Evaluate \(\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\).
blocks.explanation: \(\sin\frac{3\pi}{4} = \sin\left(\pi - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), so \(\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \sin^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\pi}{4}\) (not \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\), which is outside \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\)).

book_ref.quote: must lie between \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{2}\)

blocks.prompt: 8 Does \(\sin^{-1}\frac{\pi}{2}\) exist? Give a reason.
blocks.explanation: No. \(\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.571 > 1\), and the domain of \(\sin^{-1}\) is \([-1, 1]\); no angle has sine greater than \(1\). (Do not confuse it with \(\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\).)

book_ref.quote: does not exist, because no angle has sine 2

blocks.prompt: 9 The point \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}, -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\) lies on the principal sine graph. Write the matching point on \(y = \sin^{-1} x\) and the line in which the two graphs are mirror images.
blocks.explanation: Coordinates swap: \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, -\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\), because \(\sin^{-1}\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{3}\). The graphs are mirror images in the line \(y = x\).

book_ref.quote: Every point \((a, b)\) of \(y = \sin x\) gives the point \((b, a)\) of \(y = \sin^{-1} x\)

blocks.prompt: 10 Name two intervals, other than \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), on which the sine function is one-to-one with range \([-1, 1]\).
blocks.explanation: Any \(\left[n\pi - \frac{\pi}{2}, n\pi + \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\): e.g. \(\left[\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right]\) (\(n = 1\), sine decreasing) and \(\left[-\frac{3\pi}{2}, -\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) (\(n = -1\)).

book_ref.quote: where it is strictly increasing or decreasing, to make the sine function one-to-one

blocks.prompt: 11 Define the principal cosine function and the inverse cosine function, with domain and range.
blocks.explanation: Principal cosine function: \(\cos : [0, \pi] \to [-1, 1]\), bijective. Inverse cosine: \(y = \cos^{-1} x\) iff \(x = \cos y\); domain \([-1, 1]\), range \([0, \pi]\).

book_ref.quote: is called the principal cosine function

blocks.prompt: 12 Why is the cosine function restricted to \([0, \pi]\) and not to \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\)?
blocks.explanation: Cosine is even: \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\), so on \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) it is not one-to-one, and it is never negative there (not onto \([-1, 1]\)). On \([0, \pi]\) it falls from \(1\) to \(-1\), taking each value once.

book_ref.quote: Why not use \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) again, as for sine?

blocks.prompt: 13 Evaluate \(\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)\).
blocks.explanation: \(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}\), so the value is \(\cos^{-1}\frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi}{3}\) (not \(-\frac{\pi}{3}\), which is outside \([0, \pi]\)).

book_ref.quote: Cosine is an even function, so a negative angle and the matching positive angle always give the same value.

blocks.prompt: 14 Evaluate \(\cos^{-1}\left(\sin\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)\).
blocks.explanation: \(\sin\frac{7\pi}{6} = -\frac{1}{2}\). The angle in \([0, \pi]\) with cosine \(-\frac{1}{2}\) is \(\pi - \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{2\pi}{3}\).

book_ref.quote: Look at the negative inputs in the table: they give obtuse angles.

blocks.prompt: 15 Which is larger, \(\cos^{-1}(0.2)\) or \(\cos^{-1}(0.7)\)? Give a reason without a calculator.
blocks.explanation: \(\cos^{-1}(0.2)\). The graph of \(\cos^{-1} x\) falls from \((-1, \pi)\) to \((1, 0)\): it is a decreasing function, so the smaller number \(0.2\) has the larger angle.

book_ref.quote: A larger number has a smaller angle.

blocks.prompt: 16 Write the domain and range of \(f(x) = \tan x\), and explain why some points are left out of the domain.
blocks.explanation: Domain: \(\left\{x \mid x \in \mathbb{R},\ x \ne (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2},\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\); range: \(\mathbb{R}\). Since \(\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\) and \(\cos x = 0\) at the odd multiples of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), division by zero would occur there.

book_ref.quote: Division by zero is not defined, so these points are not in the domain.

blocks.prompt: 17 Define the principal tangent function and the inverse tangent function, with domain and range.
blocks.explanation: Principal tangent function: \(\tan : \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \to \mathbb{R}\), bijective. Inverse tangent: \(y = \tan^{-1} x\) iff \(x = \tan y\); domain \((-\infty, \infty)\), range \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

book_ref.quote: is called the principal tangent function

blocks.prompt: 18 Find the principal value of \(\tan^{-1}\left(\tan\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\).
blocks.explanation: \(\tan\frac{2\pi}{3} = -\tan\frac{\pi}{3} = -\sqrt{3}\). A negative value gives a negative angle in \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\): \(\tan^{-1}(-\sqrt{3}) = -\frac{\pi}{3}\).

book_ref.quote: Use the sign and the principal range to place the angle

blocks.prompt: 19 Why is the range of \(\tan^{-1} x\) an open interval, while the range of \(\sin^{-1} x\) is closed?
blocks.explanation: \(\tan\left(\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) is undefined, so \(\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\) cannot be values of \(\tan^{-1} x\): range \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). But \(\sin\left(\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \pm 1\) exist, so \(\sin^{-1}(\pm 1) = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}\) and its range is \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).

book_ref.quote: Why an open interval this time (round brackets)?

blocks.prompt: 20 Write the asymptotes of the graphs of the principal \(y = \tan x\) and of \(y = \tan^{-1} x\).
blocks.explanation: Principal \(y = \tan x\): vertical asymptotes \(x = -\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\). \(y = \tan^{-1} x\): horizontal asymptotes \(y = -\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(y = \frac{\pi}{2}\) (reflection in \(y = x\) swaps the coordinates).

book_ref.quote: the coordinates swap, so vertical lines turn into horizontal lines

blocks.prompt: 21 Write the domain and range of \(f(x) = \csc x\) and explain the range.
blocks.explanation: Domain: \(\{x \mid x \in \mathbb{R},\ x \ne n\pi,\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\) (where \(\sin x \ne 0\)). Range: \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1) = (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\), because \(|\sin x| \le 1\) gives \(|\csc x| = \frac{1}{|\sin x|} \ge 1\).

book_ref.quote: the reciprocal always has size at least 1

blocks.prompt: 22 Define the principal cosecant function and give the domain and range of the inverse cosecant function.
blocks.explanation: Principal cosecant: \(\csc : \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \to (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\), bijective. \(y = \csc^{-1} x \iff x = \csc y\); domain \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)\), range \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).

book_ref.quote: called principal cosecant function

blocks.prompt: 23 Find the principal value of \(\csc^{-1}\left(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\).
blocks.explanation: \(\csc y = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\) means \(\sin y = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) with \(y \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), so \(y = -\frac{\pi}{3}\).

book_ref.quote: A quick example of our own. Find

blocks.prompt: 24 Why is \(0\) not in the range of \(\csc^{-1} x\)?
blocks.explanation: \(\csc^{-1} x = 0\) would mean \(x = \csc 0 = \frac{1}{\sin 0}\), which is undefined. So \(0\) is removed; on the graph, \(y = 0\) is a horizontal asymptote of \(y = \csc^{-1} x\).

book_ref.quote: That is why 0 is not in the range.

blocks.prompt: 25 Define the principal secant function and give the domain and range of the inverse secant function.
blocks.explanation: Principal secant: \(\sec : \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cup \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right] \to (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\), bijective. \(y = \sec^{-1} x \iff x = \sec y\); domain \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)\), range \(\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cup \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]\).

book_ref.quote: is called principal secant function

blocks.explanation: \(\sec y = \sqrt{2} \Rightarrow \cos y = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), \(y \in [0, \pi]\): \(\sec^{-1}\sqrt{2} = \frac{\pi}{4}\). \(\sec y = -1 \Rightarrow \cos y = -1\): \(\sec^{-1}(-1) = \pi\).

book_ref.quote: negative angles are outside the range of

blocks.prompt: 27 Write the range of \(\sec^{-1} x\) and explain why \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) is not in it.
blocks.explanation: Range: \(\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cup \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]\). \(\sec\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{1}{\cos(\pi/2)} = \frac{1}{0}\) is undefined, so no \(x\) has \(\sec^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}\); \(y = \frac{\pi}{2}\) is a horizontal asymptote.

book_ref.quote: Including \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) in the range

blocks.prompt: 28 Which interval does the principal \(\sec\) function use, and which does the principal \(\csc\) function use? What is removed from each?
blocks.explanation: \(\sec\) uses cosine's interval \([0, \pi]\) with \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) removed (\(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0\)); \(\csc\) uses sine's interval \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) with \(0\) removed (\(\sin 0 = 0\)).

book_ref.quote: uses cosine's interval \([0, \pi]\)

blocks.prompt: 29 Define the principal cotangent function and give the domain and range of the inverse cotangent function.
blocks.explanation: Principal cotangent: \(\cot : (0, \pi) \to (-\infty, \infty)\), bijective. \(y = \cot^{-1} x \iff x = \cot y\); domain \((-\infty, \infty)\), range \((0, \pi)\).

book_ref.quote: called principal cotangent function

blocks.explanation: \(\cot\frac{\pi}{4} = 1\), so \(\cot^{-1} 1 = \frac{\pi}{4}\). \(\cot\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\cos(\pi/3)}{\sin(\pi/3)} = \frac{1/2}{\sqrt{3}/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(\cot^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{\pi}{3}\); both lie in \((0, \pi)\).

book_ref.quote: So \(\cot^{-1} x\) is always strictly between 0 and \(\pi\)

blocks.prompt: 31 Find the value of \(\cos\left[\sin^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right]\).
blocks.explanation: Inner angle: \(\sin^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{6}\). Then \(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \cos\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

book_ref.quote: Method: work from the inside out.

blocks.prompt: 32 Find the value of \(\csc\left[\cot^{-1}(-1)\right]\).

book_ref.quote: First find the inner angle

blocks.prompt: 33 Find the value of \(\sec\left[\cot^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right]\).

book_ref.quote: Given: three expressions, each a trigonometric function of an inverse trigonometric value.

blocks.prompt: 34 Find the domain of \(f(x) = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{3} - 1\right)\).
blocks.explanation: \(-1 \le \frac{x}{3} - 1 \le 1 \Rightarrow 0 \le \frac{x}{3} \le 2 \Rightarrow 0 \le x \le 6\). Domain: \([0, 6]\).

book_ref.quote: an inverse trigonometric function only accepts inputs from its own domain

blocks.prompt: 35 Find the domain of \(g(x) = \sin^{-1}(x^{2} - 3)\).
blocks.explanation: Put the inside expression in [-1, 1] and solve both conditions.

book_ref.quote: \(\cos^{-1}\) and \(\sin^{-1}\) need the input in \([-1, 1]\)

blocks.prompt: 36 Find the domain of \(h(x) = \csc^{-1}(x - 1)\).
blocks.explanation: \(\csc^{-1}\) needs its input in \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\): \(x - 1 \le -1\) or \(x - 1 \ge 1\), i.e. \(x \le 0\) or \(x \ge 2\). Domain: \((-\infty, 0] \cup [2, \infty)\).

book_ref.quote: The table below summarizes the domains and ranges of the principal trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions.

blocks.prompt: 37 Find the domain of \(k(x) = \sec^{-1}\sqrt{x}\).
blocks.explanation: \(\sqrt{x}\) needs \(x \ge 0\), and then \(\sqrt{x} \ge 0\), so only \(\sqrt{x} \ge 1\) is possible (never \(\le -1\)): \(x \ge 1\). Domain: \([1, \infty)\).

book_ref.quote: remember any extra condition such as

blocks.prompt: 38 Find the domain of \(p(x) = \tan^{-1}(\ln x)\).
blocks.explanation: \(\tan^{-1}\) accepts every real number, so the only condition is that \(\ln x\) exists: \(x > 0\). Domain: \((0, \infty)\).

book_ref.quote: In domain questions, forgetting the domain of the inner function

blocks.prompt: 39 Is \(\cot^{-1}(-\sqrt{3}) = \tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\)? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. \(\cot^{-1}(-\sqrt{3}) = \frac{5\pi}{6}\) (range \((0, \pi)\)), but \(\tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{6}\). The relation \(\cot^{-1} x = \tan^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\) holds only for \(x > 0\); here \(\frac{5\pi}{6} = \pi + \left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\).

book_ref.quote: Parts (i) and (ii) need no such restriction because the ranges already fit.
each pair of 'co-functions' adds up to

blocks.explanation: \(\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) gives \(2\sin^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}\), so \(\sin^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{4}\) and \(x = \sin\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

book_ref.quote: Hence proved: \(\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}\)

blocks.explanation: Name the angle, find its cosine from sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, then take the reciprocal.

book_ref.quote: 7, 24, 25 is a Pythagorean triple

steps: \(\sec\alpha = \frac{29}{21}\), and \(\alpha \in \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) is in the range of \(\sec^{-1}\), so \(\alpha = \sec^{-1}\frac{29}{21}\)

blocks.prompt: 43 Without using a calculator, find \(\cos\left(\frac{1}{2}\cos^{-1}\frac{1}{8}\right)\).
blocks.explanation: Let \(\cos\alpha = \frac{1}{8}\), \(\alpha \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). \(\cos\frac{\alpha}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{1 + \cos\alpha}{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{9/8}{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{9}{16}} = \frac{3}{4}\) (positive, \(\frac{\alpha}{2}\) acute).

book_ref.quote: use the half-angle identity

blocks.text: 9.2 Sum and Difference Formulas for Inverse Trigonometric Functions

blocks.prompt: 44 State the sum and difference formulas for \(\tan^{-1}\), with the condition for each.
blocks.explanation: (v) \(\tan^{-1} x + \tan^{-1} y = \tan^{-1}\frac{x + y}{1 - xy}\), valid for \(xy < 1\). (vi) \(\tan^{-1} x - \tan^{-1} y = \tan^{-1}\frac{x - y}{1 + xy}\), valid for \(xy > -1\).

book_ref.quote: Give each inverse a name, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\)
Formula (v) needs \(1 - xy \ne 0\)

blocks.prompt: 46 Express \(\sin^{-1}\frac{4}{5} - \sin^{-1}\frac{3}{5}\) as a single inverse sine.
blocks.explanation: Formula (ii) with \(x = \frac{4}{5}\), \(y = \frac{3}{5}\) (\(xy \ge 0\)): \(x\sqrt{1 - y^{2}} - y\sqrt{1 - x^{2}} = \frac{4}{5}\cdot\frac{4}{5} - \frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{3}{5} = \frac{7}{25}\). So it equals \(\sin^{-1}\frac{7}{25}\).

book_ref.quote: (ii) Same start as (i), but use

blocks.prompt: 47 Express \(2\tan^{-1}\frac{2}{3}\) as a single inverse tangent.

book_ref.quote: Further by putting \(y = x\) in (v), we get

blocks.prompt: 48 Show that \(2\tan^{-1} 2 \ne \tan^{-1}\frac{2 \cdot 2}{1 - 2^{2}}\). Which condition fails?
blocks.explanation: \(\tan^{-1}\frac{4}{-3} = \tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{4}{3}\right)\) is negative, but \(2\tan^{-1} 2\) is positive (about \(2.214\), more than \(\frac{\pi}{2}\)). The double formula needs \(-1 < x < 1\); here \(x = 2\).

book_ref.quote: becomes \(x^{2} < 1\), that is \(-1 < x < 1\)

blocks.explanation: Join the left side with formula (v), solve, then test each root.

book_ref.quote: so every root must be tested in the original equation

blocks.prompt: 50 Use formula (iii) to evaluate \(\cos^{-1}\frac{1}{2} + \cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\), and check the answer.

book_ref.quote: (iii) Let \(\cos^{-1}x = \alpha\), \(\cos^{-1}y = \beta\)

blocks.prompt: 51 With \(x = \frac{1}{2}\), show that \(\sin^{-1} x + \sin^{-1} x \ne \sin^{-1}(2x)\).
blocks.explanation: Left side: \(\frac{\pi}{6} + \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{3}\). Right side: \(\sin^{-1} 1 = \frac{\pi}{2}\). Not equal; the correct result is \(2\sin^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\left(2x\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\right) = \sin^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\pi}{3}\).

book_ref.quote: Inverse functions do not add like that

blocks.prompt: 52 Verify \(\cos^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\) for \(x = \frac{3}{5}\), and show that it fails for \(x = -\frac{3}{5}\).
blocks.explanation: \(x = \frac{3}{5}\): \(\sqrt{1 - \frac{9}{25}} = \frac{4}{5}\), and \(\cos^{-1}\frac{3}{5} = \sin^{-1}\frac{4}{5}\) (same acute angle). \(x = -\frac{3}{5}\): \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{3}{5}\right)\) is obtuse \(\left(= \pi - \sin^{-1}\frac{4}{5}\right)\), but \(\sin^{-1}\frac{4}{5}\) is acute. It holds only for \(0 \le x \le 1\).

book_ref.quote: The same triangle idea turns any inverse function into another.
